pages.text: It Took 20,000 Shots to Capture This Extraordinary Moment in Nature | National Geographic PHOTOGRAPHY It Took 20,000 Shots to Capture This Extraordinary Moment in Nature After two decades following monarch butterflies across North America, Nat Geo photographer Jaime Rojo shares the remarkable stories behind his images—and the fleeting moments he spent years trying to capture. In Monarchs , photographer Jaime Rojo brings together two decades of stunning images documenting one of nature’s most extraordinary migrations, from the forests of Mexico to the fields of the American Midwest, revealing the beauty, chaos, and wonder of these remarkable butterflies. By Alexa Robles-Gil Photographs by Jaime Rojo Published October 16, 2026 In February 2004, Jaime Rojo , a young Spanish photographer, was walking uphill in Sierra Chincua, a forested mountain range in Mexico that doubles as a sanctuary for the tens of millions of monarch butterflies that migrate there each winter. As he climbed with the friends who had brought him, he began to spot monarchs along the path. Only a few at first. But the higher he went, the more he heard a sound in the background, like something whispering in the trees. Suddenly, a swarm of butterflies was flying overhead, millions of orange and black wings fluttering against the blue sky beyond. “There were so many that you could feel a slight breeze when they flew over you,” he says. Close j333-1145's Diary osm 极简画法 Posted by j333-1145 on 3 May 2026 in Chinese (China) (‪中文(中国大陆)‬) . 前言 这些随想是在去年年底写的，也许对其他 mapper 有启发，故发布。 以下经验会让画 osm 变得高效、美观、简洁，避免 无线细化 。 正文 osm 本质是抽象、简化的地图，所以画面元素要少、整洁。增加过多的元素会导致地图画面杂乱无章、不美观，而且后期维护也很繁琐。 例：一条公路的两旁有人行道，除非有物理隔离（比如栏杆），否则推荐在道路上加 sidewalk=both ，而不是把两旁的人行道都画出来 要提炼出对象特征，想出表达完整又简练的画面布局，同时不要出现渲染错误。 直线要直、圆形要园、方形要方、弧线要优雅大气。 线条不宜有过多节点，尽量把多余的、又不影响整体的节点删掉 道路、河流、森林等图画，宜大不宜小，宜长不宜短，宜整不宜碎 能不重叠就不重叠。如果一片区域（比如小区、医院、学校等），有明确的边界（比如围墙），最好先画完内部道路、建筑设施，最后再画上土地利用 area=yes 。否则就不要画。 一般使用 iD 编辑器最简单。若想画整齐的方形建筑物建议用 JOSM，并使用 building 插件。 标签方面，非必要不多加。 Discussion Comment from 真中あお on 3 July 2026 at 09:23 提醒自己地图是对现实的抽象，不追求无限细化，这是很有意义的方法论d(`･∀･)b Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

Peter Van Breukelen/Redferns/Redferns hide caption toggle caption i Peter Van Breukelen/Redferns/Redferns Jack DeJohnette , one of the most daring and dynamic jazz drummers of the last 60 years, with a loose-limbed yet exacting beat that propelled a limitless range of adventurous music, died on Sunday at HealthAlliance Hospital in Kingston, N.Y. He was 83. The cause was congestive heart failure, Lydia DeJohnette, his wife and manager, tells NPR. DeJohnette had a singular voice at the drums: earthy and elastic, instantly recognizable. Rather than focus the articulation of tempo on his ride cymbal, he often distributed his emphasis around the drum set. He adapted this flowing approach from modern jazz innovators like Roy Haynes as well as avant-garde pioneers like Rashied Ali , devising what he called a multidirectional style. Putting aside the breathtaking exhibitions of physical and psychological intensity it can produce, the sport has long been a refuge of the underclass, credited with changing the lives of the disenfranchised and impoverished. In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime." pages.description: James Botham is accustomed to working away from the spotlight, but his performance could not be denied against New Zealand.
pages.text: James Botham: Wales' unlikely hero in historic win over New Zealand - BBC Sport Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, James Botham was man of the match in Wales' historic win over New Zealand By Gareth Rhys Owen BBC Sport Wales Published 16 November 2026 James Botham lay sprawled on the Principality Stadium turf, pain and exhaustion etched across his face. Whenever the whistle blew, the Wales flanker in the red scrum cap took an age to rise. Precious seconds to recover. Nobody counts tackles when the ball is dead. But when play resumed, he was everywhere. Tackling, scrambling, hitting the deck and springing back up. By the final whistle, Botham had helped Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years. He was man of the match. And as the celebrations began, the tears flowed. Quite an afternoon for a player accustomed to working away from the spotlight. Keeping a Botham out of the headlines was always going to be difficult. His grandfather, Lord Ian Botham , is one of Britain's great sporting celebrities. Outspoken, charismatic and capable of turning cricket matches almost single-handedly, he is box-office. James is different. His game is built on tackles, chasing, wrestling and relentless graft. Few positions in rugby are less glamorous than blind-side flanker. But on Saturday, Wales' number six was the star of the show. DeWitt characterized people of Japanese ancestry during World War II. He insisted that even those who had been born and raised as U.S. citizens nevertheless posed a threat because their Japanese “racial strains” were “undiluted.” Under the authority of President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Executive Order 9066, DeWitt ordered the removal of all Japanese Americans from the West Coast in 1942. Allowed to take only what they could carry, they were imprisoned, without trial, in some of the most desolate places in the country. Today, the National Park Service preserves those sites so that visitors may learn their story. He is an Honors College graduate of Ball State University and a graduate of the Indiana University School of Law. During law school, Novak worked as a law clerk for Bill Cummings, formerly the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia. Close jfd553's Diary Mapping Icefields Parkway, Part 1: A two-year mapping journey Posted by jfd553 on 4 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 6 November 2026. I spent two years mapping the areas surrounding one of the most beautiful drives in the world. Each morning, I looked forward to discovering and mapping an area adjacent to a one I did the day before. This diary entry serves as an introduction to a series of texts covering the challenges I encountered and how I overcame them. Included below are a few snapshots taken in the field, which capture the majestic landscapes along the Icefields Parkway. I have also added a “before and after” map excerpt, as well as a short video, to illustrate how my work gradually took shape over time. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. The parkway, which is a 232 km stretch of highway cutting through Banff and Jasper National Parks, attracts between 1.2 million and 2 million visitors per year. The parkway offers exceptional alpine landscape, with glaciers, rivers, turquoise lakes, and breathtaking mountain views directly from the roadside (Figure 1). Best of all, many of these landmarks can be reached in a single day’s hike (Figure 2). Figure 1: North Saskatchewan River alongside the parkway. pages.text: Join Open Jam Sessions for an Insight Into London's Grassroots Music Scene | National Geographic TRAVEL Join Open Jam Sessions for an Insight Into London's Grassroots Music Scene Across the city, a growing crop of music-making events is nourishing the capital’s grassroots music scene — and helping to alleviate loneliness in the process. The Five Points Jam brings together more than 30 musicians for high-energy performances. Richard Mukuze By Sam Kemp Published November 18, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The jazz saxophonist Stan Getz once said that the best music sounds “like a good conversation among friends”. Right now, some of the most interesting musical conversations in London are happening at its grassroots venues, where open jam sessions are giving musicians of all levels a platform to improvise, hone their craft and form new friendships. Participants may not know their fellow musicians, let alone the genre or dynamic, so there’s no choice but to embrace whatever the night brings. It’s about getting lost in music, together. London’s open jam scene really took hold in the years following the Covid lockdown — a period when music-lovers were looking for new ways to connect in a city beset by independent venue closures and the ongoing effects of social isolation. The Five Points Project, an events platform founded in 2022 by school friends James Lear and Max Riby-Williams, offered a solution: find a space, fill it with musicians and watch a community take shape. pages.text: Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand | National Geographic TRAVEL Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand A new off-grid tour takes travellers deep into New Zealand’s largest basin in search of the elusive black stilt. New Zealand's Southern Alps are home to one of the world's rarest birds: the black stilt. Natasha Bazika By Natasha Bazika Published June 11, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Clouds move quickly across the Mackenzie Basin, dragging shadows over braided riverbeds and dry tussock plains that stretch towards New Zealand’s Southern Alps. One moment, the landscape is washed silver; the next, it disappears beneath a sweep of weather rolling over the mountains. I’m heading deeper into this high country on a window of borrowed time, crossing the 46,950-acre wilderness of Glenmore Station, a merino sheep, deer and cattle station. Hours earlier, the same storm front had grounded my helicopter flight to the country’s highest whisky bar — The Bad Decision, on a saddle above Glenmore Station — before it could leave the tarmac. Now, I’m racing a temporary clearing in the weather to find something far more elusive than a dram of mountain liquor: the black stilt, or kakī in Māori, one of the rarest birds on the planet. “The Mackenzie Basin has its own weather system,” says guide Ben Laffan, who’s taking me on Tekapo Adventures’ Black Stilt birding tour , a newly launched birdwatching experience, directing our four-wheel drive up a rough track. Juanes & Mon Laferte: Tiny Desk Concert May 23, 2018 5:00 AM ET Felix Contreras Credit: NPR Colombian pop star Juanes and Chilean singer Mon Laferte recently wrapped up a sold-out tour of the United States, which (lucky for us) included a stop at the Tiny Desk. Laferte began the concert solo with the torch song "Pa' Dónde Se Fue" (Where Did You Go?). She sang the break-up story with a smirk that belied the heartache hiding in her poignant lyrics. Then, after a short set break starring the Tiny Desk engineer Josh Rogosin, Juanes joined her to perform the duo's sultry single, "Amárrame" (Tie Me Up). It's rare to see Juanes in such an intimate setting. After almost two decades of performing solo, the Latin pop star is more of a stadium and arena kind of guy. It's a treat to hear his voice unencumbered by loud speakers or crowd noise, and to see his facial expressions as he sings lyrics that many of us know by heart. This marked a return to the intimacy that fueled his earliest days and that's still present in the personal lyrics that have sold millions of records. Sponsor Message That intimacy was heightened by the presence of Laferte. The duo performed a PG-13 version of "Amárrame," a passionate pop song with lyrics reminiscent of 50 Shades Of Grey . That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race. The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris. But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances. This weekend, I was at State of the Map 2026, the international OpenStreetMap conference, which took place in Paris this year. Here’s a brief, personal feedback and a round-up of a few presentations that stood out for me. You can also find all the videos at https://peertube.openstreetmap.fr . NB: there is a French version here . This one was translated with the help of DeepL translate. The most inspiring: cartes.app Inspiring: cartes.app is a slightly mad project aimed at creating a new Google Maps, but without its car-centric bias. It started with a single contributor, but he’s managed to build a strong team around him: he has the insight to use the best open-source software components for his project – MapLibre for map navigation, vector tiles for map rendering, Photon for geocoding, and Transitious for public transport. Today, the developer is no longer working alone: he is securing funding and attracting contributors from around the world to improve his app and translate it so it can reach a global audience. It’s a wonderful project worth supporting, and you can do so by subscribing to cartes.app premium for just €1 a month. Jungle: Tiny Desk Concert November 2, 2026 5:00 AM ET Robin Hilton Credit: Photo: Lexy Beale/NPR It's hard for any band to make the old sound completely new, but Jungle has spent much of the past decade transforming vintage soul and R&B into something almost alien. The grooves are deep and warmly familiar, with wistful reflections on love and longing. But even in the brightest moments, there's often a thread of mystery and melancholy that leaves you questioning whether everything is as it seems. Fronted by the trio of Tom McFarland, Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto, Jungle is known for fluid live sets, with songs that spill into each other. True to form, at the Tiny Desk, they perform more than a half-dozen tracks that run together in a single, continuous groove. "We're gonna keep the music rolling," Lloyd-Watson tells the NPR crowd as the band melts seamlessly from 2018's "Beat 54 (All Good Now)" into "Dominoes" from the 2023 album Volcano. Sponsor Message The members are all smiles here, even as they sing about faded dreams ("Casio"), dead-end infatuations ("Someday, Somewhere") and the struggle to hold on when everything falls apart ("The Wave"). Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse Outstanding Natural Area In northern Palm Beach County on Florida’s urbanized Treasure Coast lies the 120-acre Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse Outstanding Natural Area (ONA). The ONA was designated by Congress in 2008 for the preservation, protection and enhancement of seven key resources and values found on the site; these include the remarkable biodiversity and rich history of the site. The site is the only unit of the National Conservation Lands east of the Mississippi River, and the only unit managed by the BLM’s Eastern States. About The ONA is home a remarkable array of natural and cultural resources including four sensitive habitats, 26 special status species, and an archaeological record providing evidence of human occupation dating back over 5,000 years. These historic, cultural and natural resources serve as the bases on which the Congressional designation directs the protection, preservation and enhancement of the sites key values. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. Justin Bis Justin Bis is the Chief of Staff for the Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC) at the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). In this role, he works alongside OTC leadership to maximize the impact of DOE’s investments in technology commercialization, strengthen coordination across the agency, and ensure long-term success. Mr. Bis has more than a decade of experience in government service and public life. He previously served at the White House as Special Assistant to President Trump and Deputy Director of the Presidential Personnel Office, where he managed the appointment of senior government officials responsible for regulating the U.S. financial and energy markets. At DOE, he was the Director of Intergovernmental and External Affairs under Secretary Dan Brouillette, serving as the department’s primary liaison to trade associations, labor unions, and state, local, and tribal governments. Beyond his federal service, Mr. Bis was the Executive Director of the Ohio Republican Party and Ohio Deputy State Director for the Donald J. Trump for President campaign. He holds a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from Northern Michigan University.

Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn K2-Play Completes Final Phase of North Fruita Desert Trails Master Plan Oct 15, 2026 FRUITA, Colo. – Over the past eight years, the North Fruita Desert has changed in ways riders can see as soon as they arrive. There are more miles of singletrack, more places to camp and dedicated space for races and other large events, all part of a broader effort by the Bureau of Land Management and community partners to keep pace with one of western Colorado’s busiest recreation areas. This fall, the final trail in the North Fruita Desert Trails Master Plan is complete. K2-Play winds for about three miles along the base of the Book Cliffs and completes the final phase of a roughly 30-mile expansion of the 18 Road trail system. Its completion caps years of planning and construction involving the BLM Grand Junction Field Office, Colorado Plateau Mountain Bike Trail Association, Mesa County, City of Fruita, local businesses, professional trail builders and volunteers. In this role, Kaveh leads the Department of Energy’s international portfolio and advances President Trump’s vision of American energy dominance as a force for global prosperity and stability. He works with America’s allies and partners to expand markets for American energy and technology, strengthen energy security, counter malign foreign influence, and promote access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy around the world. Kaveh previously served in DOE’s Office of International Affairs, where he led U.S. energy engagement with the Arabian Peninsula and West Africa. In a judicial review claim, Nicola Hayden argues the EA has failed to carry out its legal duties to prevent the pollution of bathing sites on the Romney Marsh coast in Kent, including at the Littlestone and Dymchurch beaches which have a "poor" water quality rating. She said the community had been "fighting for change for years" but there was "still no comprehensive action plan to find the root causes and fix them". The EA said as the matter was subject to ongoing legal proceedings, it was unable to comment at this stage. pages.title: Khawaja book: Sandpapergate a stench Cricket Australia cannot shake - BBC Sport
pages.description: Usman Khawaja's autobiography has exposed the limbo Australian cricket finds itself stuck in over the sandpaper scandal, writes Stephan Shemilt.
pages.text: Khawaja book: Sandpapergate a stench Cricket Australia cannot shake - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pat Cummins has led Australia in 43 Tests since 2021 By Stephan Shemilt Cricket Correspondent Published 10 November 2026 There are stories that can damage reputations, tarnish legacies and put asterisks next to achievements. Never-ending sagas, claim and counterclaim, one word against another. Are Pep Guardiola's trophies at Manchester City rendered worthless by financial rule breaches? Would either of the Houston Astros or Boston Red Sox have won the World Series without sign stealing? How much fake blood was spilled by Harlequins? Now, sandpapergate has morphed into Usman Khawaja's-book-gate, opening old wounds and asking questions that have hung over Australian cricket since Cameron Bancroft hid some DIY equipment in his jockstrap in 2018. Published on Tuesday, Khawaja's autobiography – Sabr – is only suggesting what plenty have suspected for the past eight years. It always seemed likely that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were not the only three members of the Australia camp with knowledge of the sandpaper plot. Careful with his words, perhaps for legal reasons, Khawaja has said enough to reignite a row that once consumed the entire nation of Australia. Crucially, the former batter has not named individuals and, in the opinion of Cricket Australia (CA), not presented enough evidence to merit a new investigation. During this week, academia, industry, non-profit organizations, and government agencies host events, share resources, provide trainings, and engage community to build awareness about the cybersecurity job opportunities, educate people on how to develop capabilities to qualify for cybersecurity roles, and showcase how building a cybersecurity workforce enhances the Nation’s security and promotes economic prosperity. Kimberly Ballou Kimberly Ballou serves as Chief of Staff for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of International Affairs (IA), a role she resumed in June 2026 after previously serving in the position during a period of leadership transition in early 2025. She has more than two decades of experience advancing U.S. international energy policy, global energy security, strategic partnerships, and international cooperation. Throughout her career, Kimberly has held senior leadership positions across IA, including Senior Advisor for Strategic Operations to the IA Assistant Secretary, Acting Director for Asian Affairs, Deputy Director for American Affairs, and Senior Advisor for Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. Kimberly has also served in multiple overseas leadership assignments as Acting Energy Attaché and DOE Office Director, including at the U.S. Embassy in Paris, France; U.S. Embassy in Mexico City, Mexico; and U.S. Mission to the OECD in Paris, where she represented DOE and advanced engagement with foreign governments and key multilateral organizations, including the International Energy Agency and Nuclear Energy Agency. Phil Westcott From Juneau, to Anchorage, to Nome, and beyond, people in Alaska are often spotted wearing a colorful or patterned hooded garment with a big front pocket. This classic Alaska attire is known as a kuspuk. Kuspuk is an English word based on the Indigenous Yup’ik word “qaspeq” which translates to “cloth over parka.” The original qaspeq was made from gut skin, animal hide, or feathered bird skin to keep the wearer warm and dry—a constant struggle known all too well by those who have live, work, and travel in the arctic. In the 1800s, European whalers brought goods to trade, which included cloth bags filled with flour or sugar. Indigenous (Inupiaq/Yup’ik) women repurposed the cotton flour sacks and sewed a lightweight summer garment that resembled the “over parkas” worn in the winter.Today, kuspuks are often made of colorful or patterned cotton material and are locally hand-made. The area is known for the great number of hump-backed flute player images and a great variety of bird figures. The site is also of interest to those tracing the route of El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, as the ancient road passed along here as well. Si no hay agua y jabón disponibles, usar un desinfectante de manos con al menos un 60 por ciento de alcohol puede matar estos microbios. Lab-Embedded Entrepreneurship Program (OTC) What is LEEP? The U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC) Lab-Embedded Entrepreneurship Program (LEEP) recruits the best and brightest through a national call for a two-year funded fellowship. This fellowship provides innovators who have early-stage energy startups and/or emerging technologies with the support needed to develop and transition their ideas into the market. These entrepreneurs are embedded for a period of two years at one of four national labs where they are mentored by a lab scientist. LEEP also provides support at the local, regional, and national levels including entrepreneurship training and a networking ecosystem to address the hurdles traditionally faced by early-stage energy and manufacturing technology startups. What are the impacts of LEEP? The U.S. makes major investments in basic and applied energy and manufacturing research, at both universities and DOE National Labs. The list becomes effective each October 1, and remains in effect through the following September 30. The reference period used in preparing the current list was January 2024 through December 2025. The national average unemployment rate (including Puerto Rico) during this period is rounded to 4.16 percent. Twenty percent higher than the national unemployment rate during this period is rounded to 5 percent. Since 5 percent is below the minimum 6.0 percent, a civil jurisdiction must have a two-year unemployment rate of 6.0 percent or higher in order to be classified an LSA.
